structure.title: The proposed escape
structure.text: Crito arrives with practical arrangements and urgent reasons for Socrates to leave. The conversation begins with friendship under pressure.

structure.title: Testing the obligation
structure.text: Socrates asks which reasons should govern action, then imagines the city's laws addressing him. The imagined speech must itself be examined.

people.name: Crito
people.text: Socrates' old and wealthy friend, who has bribed the guards and arranged an escape, and comes at dawn to beg him to take it.

people.name: Socrates
people.text: The philosopher, condemned to death and awaiting execution, who will only leave prison if an argument shows him he should.

people.name: The Laws
people.text: The laws of Athens, imagined by Socrates as speaking to him, who ask whether a lifelong citizen may break them when they turn against him.

context.title: Injury and response
context.text: Socrates distinguishes suffering injustice from being entitled to commit it. Crito must show that escape would be right, not merely understandable.
context.takeaway: A wrong verdict does not settle every question.

context.title: Consent to a city
context.text: The Laws connect residence and civic benefits with obligations. Whether those connections establish consent is part of the argument's difficulty.
context.takeaway: Examine the terms of the supposed agreement.

notice.text: Separate public reputation from good reasons.
notice.why: Crito and Socrates assign different authority to opinion.
Giving the Laws a voice changes the emotional force of the case.

opening: The escape has been arranged. Money is available, friends will help, and Socrates can leave prison before his execution. Crito cannot understand why he hesitates: staying will abandon his children and make his friends look cowardly. Socrates insists that a wrongful sentence does not settle whether escaping would be right. In a conversation with almost no room left for abstraction, Plato makes a man account for his obligations to the city that has condemned him, while someone who loves him begs him to live.
